strengths: L4Q addresses a practical NLP deployment problem: quantizing the combined pretrained weights and LoRA updates allows adaptation under the inference quantizer while eliminating the separate high-precision adapter branch.

The evaluation covers several model families, sizes from 3B to 33B, and both 3-bit and 4-bit quantization. Some improvements are substantial: on 3-bit LLaMA-2 7B, commonsense accuracy reaches 61.3%, compared with 57.4% for QAT-LoRA and 56.3% for QA-LoRA.

The reported systems results demonstrate useful potential. For 7B training, L4Q uses 25.4 GB versus 79.5 GB for conventional QAT and 25.1 GB for LoRA. Measurements using an actual inference kernel support the benefit of eliminating the adapter branch.
The appendices provide task-level results, optimizer settings, and initialization, rank, and group-size ablations. These help assess the method beyond aggregate accuracy.
weaknesses: Baseline fidelity needs clarification. QLoRA and LoftQ are modified to use uniform quantization, so the comparisons do not establish superiority over their original configurations. Additionally, the blanket statement that adapters use Kaiming initialization with zero B conflicts with LoftQ's defining residual-based initialization. Its near-chance 3-bit MMLU results particularly warrant checking and documenting the implementation.

The evaluation omits a direct deployment alternative: ordinary LoRA fine-tuning followed by merging and PTQ. This would also produce an adapted model without a separate adapter branch. Comparisons against PTQ applied only to pretrained weights do not establish the advantage over this alternative.

The 33B efficiency comparison is confounded: Appendix D uses sequence length 128 specifically for L4Q, versus the stated default of 2048. Memory and time should be compared under matching workloads. Similar overall training times also depend on different training lengths; a validation-based stopping criterion would strengthen the convergence claim. L4Q's substantially higher training memory than QLoRA, 25.4 versus 7.9 GB at 7B, remains an important practical tradeoff.

Claims of consistently superior accuracy exceed the evidence. For example, on 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot, L4Q scores 50.0% versus QLoRA's 50.6%. Several other advantages are only tenths of a point, with no reported run variability or confidence intervals. Evaluation on one fine-tuning dataset and multiple-choice benchmarks also limits conclusions about general adaptation quality.

Reproducibility of the central memory optimization is insufficiently specified. The manuscript provides no L4Q implementation link or precise saved/recomputed tensor schedule, and gradient accumulation and iteration-versus-update accounting are unclear. Equations 29–30 also leave clipping-mask placement ambiguous: the elementwise weight mask must be applied before the matrix products producing adapter gradients. These implementation uncertainties and unresolved baseline questions prevent a clear Findings recommendation, despite the promising architecture and reported results.
